title: Joshua 20:1–9
context: The LORD tells Joshua to assign the cities of refuge that he had commanded through Moses (Numbers 35; Deuteronomy 19), so that a person who killed someone accidentally could flee from the avenger of blood. The person was to state his case to the city elders, live there until he stood trial before the congregation, and remain until the death of the high priest, after which he could return home. Six cities are named, three west of the Jordan and three east, spread so that refuge was within reach and available to Israelites and foreigners alike. The Greek Septuagint has a shorter form of this chapter that lacks most of verses 4–6; the WEB follows the Hebrew text. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly see here God’s justice and mercy held together, and many in both traditions see the cities as a picture of the refuge believers find in Christ (compare Hebrews 6:18), without a significant point of division between them.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Joshua, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the provision of refuge begins with the LORD speaking to Joshua. Mercy for the accidental killer is God’s own idea, not a human compromise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s initiative in providing refuge as an expression of his justice and mercy together. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing a gracious provision.

verses.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘Assign the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you by Moses,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the command to assign the cities of refuge as fulfilling what God had spoken by Moses (Numbers 35; Deuteronomy 19). God’s promises are carried out in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see continuity between the law given through Moses and its implementation under Joshua. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing God’s faithfulness to his word.

verses.text: that the man slayer who kills any person accidentally or unintentionally may flee there. They shall be to you for a refuge from the avenger of blood.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see refuge for the person who kills accidentally or unintentionally as God protecting the innocent from vengeance. Justice distinguishes between intent and accident.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the provision as upholding both the value of life and the need for just judgment (compare Exodus 21:13). Readers in both traditions commonly see the cities as showing that God cares about justice as well as protection.

verses.text: He shall flee to one of those cities, and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city, and declare his case in the ears of the elders of that city. They shall take him into the city with them, and give him a place, that he may live among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the fugitive must declare his case at the city gate, so refuge involves honesty and accountability. The elders take him in and give him a place to live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the elders’ role as part of an orderly process that protects both the fugitive and the community. Both traditions commonly see a picture of welcome extended to those who seek refuge.

verses.text: If the avenger of blood pursues him, then they shall not deliver up the man slayer into his hand; because he struck his neighbor unintentionally, and didn’t hate him before.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the refusal to hand the man slayer over to the avenger as protecting someone who struck his neighbor unintentionally. The community is responsible to uphold mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as guarding against unjust bloodshed (compare Deuteronomy 19:6, 10). Readers in both traditions commonly see the city as standing between the vulnerable and vengeance.

verses.text: He shall dwell in that city until he stands before the congregation for judgment, until the death of the high priest that shall be in those days. Then the man slayer shall return, and come to his own city, and to his own house, to the city he fled from.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the man slayer stays in the city until he stands trial and until the death of the high priest, then returns home. Some readers in both traditions see the high priest’s death as pointing to Christ, while generally holding that connection as interpretive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the two time markers, the trial and the high priest’s death, as part of a process that interpreters relate in more than one way. Many in both traditions find in the release at the high priest’s death a picture of freedom secured through Christ’s priestly work (compare Hebrews 7:24–25).

verses.text: They set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath Arba (also called Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the three cities west of the Jordan: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in Ephraim, and Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in Judah. Refuge was spread across the land so that it was within reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the careful distribution of cities as reflecting God’s concern that refuge be accessible. Readers in both traditions commonly see a picture of God’s refuge being near to all who need it.

verses.text: Beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness in the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the three cities east of the Jordan: Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan in Bashan, already named by Moses (Deuteronomy 4:41–43). The tribes beyond the Jordan also had access to refuge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuity with Moses’ earlier designation as evidence of God’s consistent purpose. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that refuge was available throughout Israel.

verses.text: These were the appointed cities for all the children of Israel, and for the alien who lives among them, that whoever kills any person unintentionally might flee there, and not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, until he stands trial before the congregation.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the inclusion of the alien who lives among them as a striking sign of God’s mercy extending beyond Israel. Refuge was open to all who needed it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as highlighting the purpose of the cities: that no one should die by the avenger’s hand before a fair trial. Many in both traditions see here a picture of believers who have fled for refuge to the hope set before them (Hebrews 6:18).
